name: Warta Thuntai
world_status: a description exists but is not accessible

sources.citation: Evans, Nicholas. 2021. The phonetics of Papuan languages in Southern New Guinea: an overview. In Kate L. Lindsey & Dineke Schokkin (eds.), Phonetic fieldwork in Southern New Guinea (Language Documentation & Conservation Special Publication 24), 5–12. Honolulu: University of Hawai'i Press.http://hdl.handle.net/10125/24991
sources.note: p. 7: regional generalisation over the 8 sampled SNG languages (Yelmek, Ngkolmpu, Nmbo, Idi, Bitur, Urama, Ende, Nen): 'no tone, no pitch accent or distinctive stress except for Urama'. Warta Thuntai is not in the sample and is not named anywhere in the chapter.

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.2 languoid page gunt1241 and OLAC page for gnt (Internet Archive copy 2026-02-02)
sources.note: Glottolog lists only Quinn 2014 as a descriptive reference (subclassification comments cite Döhler 2012 and Donohue). OLAC lists only archive material: Mary Ayres 1981 Morehead tapes (PARADISEC MA1), Evans 2012 field-methods recordings (PARADISEC GNT1, incl. a 'Phonetic transcription session' and 'Minimal pairs'), and DoBeS/TLA Morehead items 'Wartha Thuntai Field Methods Notebooks' and 'Word List: SNG Comparative List'. No published phonology.

sources.citation: Carroll, Matthew J. 2021. Phonetics and phonology of Ngkolmpu. In Lindsey & Schokkin (eds.), Phonetic fieldwork in Southern New Guinea (LD&C SP24), 33–52.http://hdl.handle.net/10125/24993
sources.note: Same Tonda-Kanum branch as Warta Thuntai but a different language (Ngkolmpu, Indonesia); the 20-page chapter has no occurrence of 'stress', 'accent' or 'prosody' at all, and does not mention Warta Thuntai.

sources.citation: Lindsey, Kate L. & Dineke Schokkin. 2021. Introduction: Phonetic fieldwork in southern New Guinea. LD&C SP24, 1–4.http://hdl.handle.net/10125/24990
sources.note: Nothing on stress; Warta Thuntai not mentioned.

sources.citation: Carroll, Matthew. 2020. The morphology of Yam languages. Oxford Research Encyclopedia of Linguistics. Oxford University Press. (ANU accepted manuscript)http://hdl.handle.net/1885/220610
sources.note: Morphology only; Table lists Warta Thuntai (other names Guntai, Kan; 430 speakers; source Quinn 2014) and the reference list gives 'Quinn, K. (2014). A description of the verbal morphology of Wartha Thuntai (Unpublished master's thesis). Australian National University.' No stress statement.

sources.citation: Evans, Nicholas. 2012. Even more diverse than we had thought: the multiplicity of Trans-Fly languages. In Nicholas Evans & Marian Klamer (eds.), Melanesian languages on the edge of Asia: challenges for the 21st century (LD&C SP5), 109–149.http://hdl.handle.net/10125/4562
sources.note: Warta Thundai data (from a Feb 2011 ANU field-methods course with speaker Sembara Dibara) appear only in Table 10 (p. 144), the paradigm of 'be'; phonology sections cover Nen and Idi only; nothing on stress in Warta Thuntai.

sources.citation: Evans, Nicholas et al. 2018. The languages of Southern New Guinea. In Bill Palmer (ed.), The languages and linguistics of the New Guinea area: a comprehensive guide, 641–774. Berlin: De Gruyter Mouton.

sources.note: The only descriptive work on the language (Glottolog's sole reference; Carroll 2020's source for the language). A 91-page ANU MA thesis on verb morphology will almost certainly open with a phonology sketch that states whether/where stress falls; Glottolog's hh record classes it med_type 'phonology or text collection'.

sources.citation: DoBeS/TLA Morehead corpus: 'Wartha Thuntai Field Methods Notebooks' (ANU field methods course, Feb–Mar 2011/2012, speaker Sembara Dibara), and PARADISEC GNT1 items 'Phonetic transcription session' (GNT1-20120301_B3) and 'Minimal pairs' (GNT1-20120215_B2).

tone.summary: Pitch or stress; a sociolinguistic survey of Tonda sub-group villages (social networks, perceived speech similarity, language vitality) with no phonological or lexical data.
